title: The One Where Eddie Moves In

jokes.text: Joey proudly shows off his new apartment decor, announcing 'Casa de Joey. I decorated it myself.'
jokes.setup: Joey excitedly presents his newly decorated apartment as if it's a masterpiece worth showing off.
jokes.punchline: The friends' visible discomfort and struggle to compliment the decor (settling on 'Art. Art it is.') reveals it's probably terrible.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey setup — his pride in something objectively bad is a reliable character beat. The friends' awkward pivot to calling it 'Art' is efficient and character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Welcome to Casa de Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Pretty nice, huh?

jokes.text: 'Well, check this out. Is it a coffee table? Is it a panther? There's no need to decide.'
jokes.setup: Joey shows off a piece of furniture/decor that apparently resembles both a coffee table and a panther.
jokes.punchline: 'There's no need to decide' — delivered with total sincerity, as if the ambiguity is a feature.
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist joke. The specificity of the two wildly different options (coffee table vs. panther) and Joey's breezy confidence that you don't need to choose is genuinely funny and perfectly Joey. The economy is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, it's... it's very... I mean, the colors are certainly...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Art.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah. Art.

jokes.text: 'So tell me, is this genuine Muppet skin?'
jokes.setup: Joey has a pillow that looks like it could be made of garish, fuzzy, puppet-like fabric.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's dry 'genuine Muppet skin' comment undercuts the decor's pretension with a darkly absurd observation.
jokes.explanation: Quintessentially Chandler — maximum wit in minimum words. 'Genuine Muppet skin' is a great specific choice; it's slightly dark (suggesting a Muppet was killed for this pillow) and very quotable. Perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Check this out! It's a chair... or is it? Could be a ottoman. Could be a small animal. Nobody knows! That's what makes it special!

jokes.text: The water table/fountain makes everyone need to urinate. 'Thanks. I love this. But you know what? It makes me want to pee.' 'Yeah, me too. I think that's the challenge.'
jokes.setup: Joey proudly shows off his water feature.
jokes.punchline: It just makes everyone immediately need to pee, and Chandler reframes the discomfort as 'the challenge' with complete seriousness.
jokes.explanation: Solid observational gag. The word 'challenge' is a funny choice — it makes peeing sound like an artistic ordeal. A competent joke that fits the apartment-tour sequence well.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is this pillow made from actual Muppets? Because I'm pretty sure I just felt Gonzo kick me in the face.

jokes.text: When asked why Chandler didn't come, someone says 'He had a thing with the... with the thing.'
jokes.setup: Friends ask where Chandler is.
jokes.punchline: The cover story falls apart immediately into the completely meaningless 'thing with the thing,' revealing that Chandler's absence is being awkwardly concealed.
jokes.explanation: A deft bit of writing — 'the thing with the thing' perfectly captures how someone sounds when they're making up an excuse on the spot. Economical and relatable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: This is a really nice water feature.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well it's making me need to pee.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is... it's working?

jokes.text: Joey has a phone in the bathroom. 'You have a phone in here?' / 'That's right. I have a phone. In here.' / 'Joey, promise me something.' / 'Yeah.' / 'Never call me from that phone.'
jokes.setup: Joey reveals a phone installed in his bathroom, clearly proud of this luxury.
jokes.punchline: The friend's deadpan request to never be called from that phone — implying they don't want to know what Joey would be doing during the call.
jokes.explanation: Strong joke with a clean structure. The bathroom phone is a perfect Joey detail, and the punchline works because it doesn't over-explain — the audience's imagination does the work. The slow, deliberate cadence of 'I have a phone. In here.' sells it further.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why didn't Chandler come see the apartment?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, he's... he's dealing with some stuff right now.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, that makes sense.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Totally.

jokes.text: Phoebe announces 'I have just been discovered.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe bursts in breathlessly with major news.
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately responds: 'Wait a minute. I claimed you in the name of France four years ago.' — Treating Phoebe as uncharted territory to be colonized.
jokes.explanation: A very sharp Chandler one-liner. The pivot from 'discovered' (talent discovery) to 'discovered' (geographic exploration/colonization) is clever misdirection. 'In the name of France' is a delightfully specific comic choice. Well-constructed and character-authentic.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And check this out - a phone in the bathroom!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, that's not impressive. A lot of people have phones in their bathrooms.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Not like this one. This is a luxury phone. It's got a really long cord.

jokes.text: Phoebe says 'Promise you won't freak out and say how great this is until I'm done,' then immediately the group cheers before she's done, and she has to keep stopping them.
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks everyone to hold their excitement until she finishes her news.
jokes.punchline: They immediately cheer after the first piece of good news, and she has to keep scolding them as more good news piles up — escalating each time.
jokes.explanation: An escalating comedic beat that works well in the room — each interruption builds on the last. Not particularly original, but executed well with the group dynamic. The structure is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, I need you to promise me something.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, what?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Promise me you won't take phone calls in the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? Why would I do that?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Because I can hear everything, and it's gross!

jokes.text: 'Oh, God, Ross, if you care about me, get the pie out of the man's hood.'
jokes.setup: The friends are celebrating Phoebe's news in the coffee shop.
jokes.punchline: Monica suddenly, urgently commands Ross to retrieve a pie from a stranger's hood — a completely unexpected non-sequitur that implies Ross has done something ridiculous off-screen.
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly specific and absurd. 'The pie out of the man's hood' is a perfect comic image — completely unexpected, yet we never see how the pie got there. The restraint in not explaining makes it funnier. Monica's urgency ('if you care about me') elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I've been discovered!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Discovered? By whom? What, like Columbus discovered America?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yes!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Phoebe, Columbus didn't discover America. The Vikings were here first. And there were already millions of people living here. So really, he just kind of... showed up.

jokes.text: 'I have to get the coffee out of that guy's pants and I'll be back in the hospital by 7.'
jokes.setup: In the chaos of the pie incident, another person apparently has coffee spilled on them.
jokes.punchline: The 'back in the hospital by 7' reveals this random bystander is a doctor or patient — giving the chaos an unexpected, darkly comic dimension.
jokes.explanation: A quick background gag that adds another chaotic layer. 'Back in the hospital by 7' is a nice dark button. Low character integration since it's a random passerby, but the economy is sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God! I got a record deal! I'm gonna be a real recording artist!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We were celebrating and I threw my pie in the air and it landed in Monica's hood.

jokes.text: 'Damn it, Ross. Get your butt out of the bathroom.' / Ross is heard blow-drying. / 'Blow-drying what? You have no hair.'
jokes.setup: Monica pounds on the bathroom door, furious that Ross has been in there for an hour.
jokes.punchline: She asks what he's blow-drying — then delivers 'You have no hair' as the punchline, implying Ross is nearly bald and making the lengthy bathroom session even more absurd.
jokes.explanation: A clean, well-timed joke with a sharp punchline. The setup is the noise of the blow dryer; the payoff is the devastating observation about Ross's hair. It works as a sibling insult and as physical comedy. Very quotable and gets a big room laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: Uh, excuse me, there's pie in my jacket pocket.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh! Yeah, sorry about that. I was just... I needed to keep it warm.

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: You put pie in MY jacket?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It seemed like a good idea at the time. Here, let me just get that for you.

jokes.text: 'It's like I'm living with him again. He's here when I go to sleep, when I wake up, when I wanna shower.' / 'I feel like I'm 16 again.'
jokes.setup: Monica complains about Ross's constant presence in her apartment.
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of 'when I go to sleep, when I wake up, when I wanna shower' culminates in the regressive 'I feel like I'm 16 again' — reframing adult cohabitation as traumatic adolescence.
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat that establishes the episode's central conflict. Functional humor but not especially clever — the sibling-regression joke is a familiar comedic territory.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I work at a coffee shop. Removing coffee from strangers' pants is literally part of my job description.

jokes.text: Rachel says 'You're both adults now' and Monica immediately screams 'Get out, you doofus!' / Rachel: 'Or, you know, he's rubber and you're glue.'
jokes.setup: Rachel tries to reason with Monica, pointing out they're both adults.
jokes.punchline: Monica instantly regresses to childish behavior ('Get out, you doofus!'), immediately undermining Rachel's point. Rachel's deadpan follow-up — 'Or, you know, he's rubber and you're glue' — is a perfect ironic button.
jokes.explanation: Great structure — the immediate contradiction of Monica's behavior proves Rachel's point wrong in the funniest possible way. Rachel's 'rubber and you're glue' callback to playground logic is a perfect ironic deadpan. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I was in there for like twenty minutes!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, you were in there for forty-five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I'm very thorough.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're thorough? It's a bathroom, not a crime scene!

jokes.text: Ross and Monica mirror each other's insults: 'Shut up.' / 'Shut up.' / 'Cut it out.' / [speaking gibberish in high-pitched voice]
jokes.setup: Ross and Monica are squabbling like children in front of the other friends.
jokes.punchline: The argument escalates to pure childish gibberish — no words at all, just mocking sounds — completing their full regression to adolescence.
jokes.explanation: Physical escalation comedy. The descent into gibberish is the logical endpoint of the sibling regression bit and lands well visually. The physical performance carries it more than the writing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to be the mature one here. I'm not going to resort to name-calling or petty insults. I'm above that.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well you're a big stupid head!

jokes.text: Rachel watches Ross and Monica act like children and says, 'I've never wanted you more.'
jokes.setup: Ross and Monica have just devolved into childish gibberish in front of Rachel.
jokes.punchline: Rachel, who is dating Ross, delivers 'I've never wanted you more' — the opposite of what you'd expect watching your boyfriend act like a child.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. Four words that are completely unexpected, perfectly ironic, and character-specific to Rachel's dry wit. The economy is almost perfect — any more words would ruin it. Big audience laugh, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know, I think the best way to resolve sibling conflict is to just talk it out like adults.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Or you could always try the classic approach: rock, paper, scissors. Best two out of three.

jokes.text: Chandler asks his slippers whether to call Joey, and the slippers bark.
jokes.setup: Chandler is lonely and talking to himself about whether to call Joey.
jokes.punchline: He asks his slippers — which apparently are novelty animal slippers — and they 'bark' in response. He then narrates: 'You know what they say: ask your slippers a question... you're going crazy.'
jokes.explanation: A great visual gag that reveals Chandler's loneliness without being maudlin. The slipper bark is absurdly funny, and Chandler's self-aware commentary ('you're going crazy') is perfectly his voice. The image of Chandler in novelty slippers consulting them is strong physical comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Back off, Monica!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, you back off! Rachel is my friend!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, but—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: But nothing! You're not going to—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Actually... that was kind of hot.

jokes.text: 'You know what they say: Ask your slippers a question... you're going crazy.'
jokes.setup: Joey has just consulted his novelty barking slippers for life advice
jokes.punchline: Joey delivers the folk-wisdom phrasing ('You know what they say') as if this is a real proverb — then the 'proverb' is just stating the obvious: you're going crazy
jokes.explanation: The joke has good structure: the setup of 'they say' implies received wisdom, and the payoff is a bathetic admission of obvious mental deterioration. Joey's self-awareness layered with his obliviousness is a nice character note.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Should I call Chandler? No, no, I shouldn't bother him. He's probably busy doing... Chandler stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Besides, my slippers told me that a true friend knows when to give space. My slippers are very wise.

jokes.text: Chandler describes his apartment as 'a regular space... fest.' on the phone with Joey, clearly struggling to sound enthusiastic.
jokes.setup: Joey asks how the apartment is doing. Chandler is clearly miserable and lonely but tries to sound upbeat.
jokes.punchline: 'A regular space-fest' — a completely made-up, meaningless phrase that conveys Chandler has absolutely nothing positive to say but is trying desperately.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Chandler character comedy. 'Space-fest' is a wonderfully empty neologism — it sounds positive but means absolutely nothing, perfectly capturing Chandler's emotional avoidance and his inability to express his true feelings. Very Chandler-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey man, what's up? I'm just... I'm doing great. Really great. Just closed a huge audition.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? That's awesome, buddy. I'm actually at a very important work thing right now. Very important.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Nice, nice. Yeah, I'm actually about to go to this incredible party. So many people want me there.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A party? Cool. Well, I should probably get back to my... my important work thing. It's very demanding.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, definitely. My party is calling. So many people. All wanting Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Right. Well, talk soon, buddy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Absolutely. Living the dream, man. Living the dream.

jokes.text: Joey and Chandler bond over the Baywatch timer — 'It's time for Baywatch!' They both shout it simultaneously
jokes.setup: An oven timer goes off during a somewhat sad phone call about their separate living situations
jokes.punchline: Both immediately and enthusiastically identify it as the Baywatch timer and shout 'Baywatch!' in unison — their old ritual perfectly preserved
jokes.explanation: Emotionally resonant comedy. The humor is that their deepest bond is a Baywatch ritual, and they don't even need to be in the same room for it to click. The simultaneous shout works as both a funny moment and a tender one — they haven't lost their connection.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What is that sound?

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: Oh, that's my Baywatch alarm. It goes off every day at this time so I don't miss it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, Baywatch! Yes!

jokes.text: 'Can you believe they gave Stephanie skin cancer?' / 'I can't believe they promoted her to lieutenant.'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey are watching Baywatch together on the phone (at their separate apartments).
jokes.punchline: They have completely different, irreconcilable priorities for what's unbelievable about the plot — one is concerned with the dramatic health storyline, the other only cares about the professional promotion.
jokes.explanation: A nice quick exchange that works on two levels: it's funny as a Baywatch joke (one of them only cares about rank) and as a character beat showing how in sync the two friends are despite being apart. Economy is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, you have cancer?

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: Yeah, but I got promoted!

jokes.text: 'You're saying that because you love Yasmine Bleeth.' / 'How could anyone not love Yasmine Bleeth?'
jokes.setup: They debate Baywatch; Chandler accuses Joey of being biased.
jokes.punchline: Joey's earnest, baffled counter — 'How could anyone not love Yasmine Bleeth?' — as if it's the most obvious truth in the universe.
jokes.explanation: A functional, period-specific joke. Joey's absolute sincerity makes it land as character comedy. A bit dated now (Yasmine Bleeth specific reference) but was likely very effective in 1996.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You see, Baywatch is a very sophisticated show. It's got drama, it's got action, it's got... people running.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And they're really good at it. Really, really good at it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: In slow motion.

jokes.text: 'Hey. Hey, they're running.' / 'See, this is the brilliance of the show. I say always keep them running.' / 'All the time running. Run. Run, Yasmine. Run like the wind.'
jokes.setup: They're watching the famous Baywatch running-on-the-beach scenes.
jokes.punchline: Joey's escalating declaration that the running is the entire genius of the show, culminating in 'Run, Yasmine. Run like the wind' — treating slow-motion beach running as high artistic philosophy.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'they're running' to 'Run like the wind' is a well-executed comedic build. Joey's earnest analysis of Baywatch's 'brilliance' is perfect character comedy — he's treating shallow television as profound. The repetition of 'run' works as a rhythmic joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't live alone. I need someone to take care of me.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't cook, I can't clean, and I'm not smart enough to live by myself.

jokes.text: 'I thought it'd be great. I figured I'd have time alone with my thoughts. But it turns out I don't have as many thoughts as you'd think.'
jokes.setup: Chandler explains why living alone isn't as great as he expected.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't have as many thoughts as you'd think' — a devastatingly self-aware admission that Chandler's interior life is emptier than expected, delivered with his signature self-deprecating logic.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and arguably one of the better Chandler lines of the series. It works on every level: the internal logic is circular and perfect ('as many thoughts as you'd think' uses 'think' in a way that highlights the joke's recursiveness), it's deeply character-specific (Chandler's self-deprecating introspection), and it's a profound-sounding way to admit intellectual emptiness. Highly quotable, near-perfectly structured.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey's finally moved on from Chandler. He's redecorating his entire apartment!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I mean, when a man starts picking out throw pillows, you know he's healed.

jokes.text: Joey's friends tell him Chandler has 'moved on' and 'decorated,' and Monica says 'Look, Chandler, he has moved on, okay? You have to, too.'
jokes.setup: Joey's friends try to console him about Chandler not wanting to be roommates again — using the exact language of a romantic breakup.
jokes.punchline: The friends speak to Joey about Chandler entirely in the language of a romantic breakup: 'he's moved on,' 'you're just friends now,' 'you're not roommates anymore.' The absurdity of treating a male friendship/roommate split as a breakup.
jokes.explanation: The sustained joke of treating Joey/Chandler's roommate split as a romantic breakup is a running comedic frame throughout the episode. It's a smart structural choice — the friends use relationship language completely earnestly. Works well.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, you guys are singing? I thought you were just... observing. Like at a zoo.

jokes.text: Phoebe starts singing 'Smelly Cat' and is immediately interrupted by a full backup singer chorus she didn't know was there. 'Oh, my God! I mean, like, who was that?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe begins her Smelly Cat recording session, singing the opening lines.
jokes.punchline: A full-throated professional backup singer chorus joins in, startling Phoebe, who had no idea they were there. Her response — 'Like, who was that?' — shows she genuinely didn't notice the backup singers literally behind her.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful Phoebe visual gag. The setup is her innocent obliviousness, and the punchline is both the dramatic entrance of the backup singers and Phoebe's failure to notice people standing literally behind her. 'Like, who was that?' is a perfect Phoebe reaction — curious, not embarrassed, completely earnest.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But don't you want to talk about the emotional reality of the song? What it means?

dialogue.speaker: Producer
dialogue.line: No. I want to talk about how many people downloaded it.

jokes.text: 'They're your backup singers. Behind you, hon.' / 'Oh. I thought they were just watching me. Like at an aquarium, you know?'
jokes.setup: The producer points out the backup singers standing right behind Phoebe.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe thought they were spectators watching her like fish in an aquarium — a completely bizarre and perfectly Phoebe interpretation of backup singers observing her.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. The aquarium metaphor is so specific and strange that it could only come from Phoebe — it reveals her worldview completely. The image of Phoebe imagining people watching her the way aquarium visitors watch fish is both absurd and character-perfect. One of the episode's best jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Actually, that's not a dinosaur at all. It's a modern reptile with anachronistic features that would never exist in the Mesozoic Era.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross, it's a cartoon.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A cartoon that's scientifically inaccurate! That's irresponsible!

jokes.text: Phoebe stops the recording to explain that the backup singers don't understand how smelly the cat actually is. 'I'm just not getting... that everyone, um, gets... how smelly this cat actually is. Maybe if we could talk about this because I need to feel that you really care about the cat.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is recording 'Smelly Cat' in a professional studio.
jokes.punchline: She stops the expensive session to give a dramatic actor's note about emotional authenticity to backup singers — treating 'Smelly Cat' as serious art requiring deep empathetic connection with the cat's odor.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant cringe comedy. Phoebe's total sincerity in treating 'Smelly Cat' with the gravity of serious artistic work is perfect. The producer's restraint makes it better — we feel the mounting cost of this conversation. 'I need to feel that you really care about the cat' is a great, highly quotable line.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Hi, is this a bad time?

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: No, not at all. I was just reorganizing my sock drawer by thread count. What's up?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, you're a big stupid head!

jokes.text: 'It's just that it's costing about $100 a minute to be in here.' / 'Oh, okay. So, um, the cat stinks, but you love it. Let's go.'
jokes.setup: The producer has been patiently listening to Phoebe's artistic concerns about emotional authenticity.
jokes.punchline: The producer reveals the financial stakes ($100/minute), and then distills Phoebe's entire artistic manifesto into 'the cat stinks, but you love it' — a hilariously reductive but accurate summary.
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy joke. The producer's brutal compression of Phoebe's artistic vision ('the cat stinks, but you love it') is a perfect punchline — it's exactly right, completely dismissive, and said without malice. The '$100 a minute' grounds the absurdity in real stakes.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Hello?

dialogue.speaker: Judy Geller
dialogue.line: Hi honey, it's Mom. I have a question for you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Hi Mom, what's up?

dialogue.speaker: Judy Geller
dialogue.line: When you and Chandler have sex, does he ever seem... satisfied?

jokes.text: 'There is no way he was a velociraptor.' / 'Look at the cranial ridge, okay? If Dino was a velociraptor, he'd have eaten the Flintstones.'
jokes.setup: Ross and Monica are arguing — but this time it's an absurd paleontological debate about the Flintstones' pet dinosaur Dino.
jokes.punchline: Ross (a paleontologist) applies rigorous scientific analysis to a cartoon dinosaur, concluding with the logically sound but absurd point that 'if Dino was a velociraptor, he'd have eaten the Flintstones.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. It's hyper-specific to Ross (a paleontologist debating cartoon dinosaurs with complete seriousness), structurally perfect, and the punchline has an internal logic that makes it feel both absurd and correct. 'He'd have eaten the Flintstones' is a great line. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: What is this? A moose hat?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I wear it sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: You wear a moose hat?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What's wrong with that?

jokes.text: Monica accidentally takes a call for Ross's girlfriend Joanna while simultaneously on the phone with Tony. She doesn't have Joanna's number. 'Did she leave a number?' / 'Did you see me write one down?' / 'I don't have her number, butt-munch.'
jokes.setup: Monica is juggling two phone calls and answering for Ross.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't have her number, butt-munch' — the word 'butt-munch' is a callback to Monica's childish regression; she's still operating at that register even after the bathroom fight.
jokes.explanation: Functional sibling comedy. 'Butt-munch' is a deliberately juvenile insult that keeps the siblings-as-children joke alive. Not a particularly strong joke on its own — the context carries it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So I met my new roommate at the butcher shop. I was standing there looking at sausages, and he goes, 'Those Italian ones are good.' So I said, 'Yeah?' And he said, 'Yeah.' And that's how we became friends.

jokes.text: 'Is that Joey guy gonna pick up his moose hat or should I toss it?' — Eddie asks, casually, about Joey's belongings.
jokes.setup: Joey comes to visit his old apartment and encounters Chandler's new roommate Eddie.
jokes.punchline: 'His moose hat' — the specificity of 'moose hat' as Joey's signature left-behind item is absurdly funny. The fact that Joey left a moose hat is perfectly Joey.
jokes.explanation: A great small moment. 'Moose hat' is the perfect detail — specific, absurd, and completely characteristic of Joey. The casualness with which Eddie asks about it adds to the sting for Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, where's my moose hat?

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: You mean that thing? I thought it was a dead animal.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It IS a dead animal!

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: Well, you should use some mousse on your hair instead. At least that won't shed all over the apartment.

jokes.text: 'Where'd you two meet?' / 'At the, uh, supermarket in the, uh, ethnic-food section.' / 'I helped him pick out a chorizo.' / (beat) 'It's a...'
jokes.setup: Joey asks how Chandler met his new roommate, hoping for an impersonal, unromantic answer.
jokes.punchline: Chandler met Eddie in the ethnic-food aisle through a chorizo — and then trails off saying 'It's a...' implying he knows how it sounds. The meeting story has the exact cadence and intimacy of how couples describe meeting each other.
jokes.explanation: Excellent continuation of the 'roommate split as romantic breakup' running gag. The chorizo detail is perfectly awkward — it sounds like a meet-cute. Chandler's 'It's a...' is the perfect embarrassed trail-off. Works great in context.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So you're living with Joey now? That's like you two are in a committed relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We prefer to think of it as a trial separation from our wives.

jokes.text: 'Oh, now it's a spare room?' / 'Well, yeah. In that it's not being used... and I have it to spare.' / 'Right.'
jokes.setup: Chandler calls Joey's old room 'a spare room,' which Joey immediately challenges.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's stilted, overly-literal definition of 'spare room' — 'not being used and I have it to spare' — is clearly defensive and rings hollow. The 'Right.' from Joey is the perfect deflated punchline.
jokes.explanation: A nice cringe beat. Chandler's defensive pseudo-logic is funny, and Joey's flat 'Right.' perfectly captures wounded dignity. The emotional subtext (Chandler trying to seem fine, failing) elevates a simple exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's me! That's my voice! It sounds so good!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, that's not you.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What do you mean? Of course that's me! I sound amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, honey, someone else is singing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well obviously that's me, I just... I've gotten better.

jokes.text: 'Hey, Joe. When'd you start using moose in your hair?' [Eddie laughing] / 'Is this guy great, or what?' / [Joey, deflated]: 'Yeah. Yeah, he is.'
jokes.setup: Joey is already hurt seeing Chandler with a new roommate. As he leaves with his moose hat, Eddie cracks a joke.
jokes.punchline: Eddie's playful 'When'd you start using moose in your hair?' gets a big laugh from Chandler — who then enthusiastically asks 'Is this guy great, or what?' to Joey, completely oblivious to how painful this is. Joey's defeated 'Yeah. Yeah, he is.' is the real punchline.
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic and emotional beat. The joke works on two levels: the wordplay ('moose in your hair' = 'mousse') and the devastating emotional layer of Chandler praising his replacement roommate to Joey's face. The two 'yeah's from Joey carry enormous deflated weight. One of the episode's strongest moments.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Phoebe, um... has anyone ever told you that your singing voice is a little... unique?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah! I get that all the time. I'm thinking of going professional.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Right, but I meant—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm gonna be huge, Ross. Huge. I can feel it.

jokes.text: 'It'll never last. He's just a rebound roommate.'
jokes.setup: Joey's friends tell him Chandler has a new roommate.
jokes.punchline: 'Rebound roommate' — applying dating vocabulary directly to roommate dynamics, fully committing to the romantic breakup metaphor.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant coinage. 'Rebound roommate' is highly quotable, perfectly economical, and represents the fullest expression of the episode's central comedic conceit. The joke does a lot of work in two words.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, you used to hate eggs. Now you're eating them every morning.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I... I don't hate them. I mean, they're not so bad when they're... prepared a certain way.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Prepared a certain way? Dude, Monica makes them the same way she always does.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, well, I'm just saying that tastes can... evolve. People change. It doesn't mean anything.

jokes.text: The Smelly Cat video plays and Phoebe realizes someone else is singing her voice. 'Oh, my God! I sound amazing!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe watches the Smelly Cat video for the first time with her friends.
jokes.punchline: A noticeably more professional, polished singing voice plays on the video — clearly not Phoebe — and Phoebe is thrilled, believing she sounds amazing. She doesn't realize it isn't her.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed cringe-comedy moment. The setup is invisible until the punchline — we don't know the voice has been dubbed until Phoebe's reaction. Her pure joy ('I sound amazing!') while the friends struggle to respond is perfectly orchestrated. High impact in a live room.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What is going on here? Every time I come home, something's different! The couch is facing a new direction, there's a new picture on the wall, you rearranged the entire kitchen!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't keep up! One day the eggs are in this cabinet, the next day they're in that cabinet. Who does that? Who IS this guy? Mr. Johnny New Eggs?!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I just want to come home and know where my eggs are going to be!

jokes.text: 'I've never heard myself sing before. I mean, except in my own head. Oh. This is so cool. Now I can hear what you hear.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe continues watching her video, moved by the singing she believes is hers.
jokes.punchline: 'Now I can hear what you hear' — Phoebe thinks her friends have always heard the professional dubbed voice, not knowing they've been listening to her actual voice (which is presumably much worse).
jokes.explanation: An exceptional layer of comedy. Phoebe's statement is doubly ironic: she thinks she's sharing in a beautiful experience with her friends, but what her friends actually hear is very different. 'Now I can hear what you hear' is heartbreaking and hilarious simultaneously — a signature Friends achievement.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: There's no juice! There's no juice! There's no juice!

jokes.text: 'Pretty, uh, different, huh?' [to Phoebe, about the dubbed singing] / 'Oh, I am sorry, but I'm incredibly talented.'
jokes.setup: Chandler tries to gently probe whether Phoebe notices the difference in the voice.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe interprets his cautious 'pretty different' as an understatement and responds with total confidence: 'I am sorry, but I'm incredibly talented.' The apology before the boast is a great small touch.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly character-integrated. Phoebe's complete, unqualified confidence in her talent — delivered with a formal 'I am sorry' as if she's correcting a factual error — is a great character joke. Quotable and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You can't like them both the same! That's like saying you like Monica and Rachel the same. Everybody has a favorite!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I really do like them equally.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, you don't! Nobody does! It's impossible!

jokes.text: Joey comes by the old apartment, acts normally, then notices the mail is now on a different table. 'You don't keep it on this table anymore?' / 'No, Eddie likes it over there.'
jokes.setup: Joey drops by his old apartment for mail. Everything looks slightly different.
jokes.punchline: The mail table has moved. A small, domestic detail — but the implication that Eddie has already rearranged Chandler's life hits Joey (and the audience) hard.
jokes.explanation: A nice cringe beat that works as both comedy and character drama. The specificity of the mail table makes Eddie's presence concrete and stinging. The restraint of making it about something so small is good writing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's not you, it's me. Actually, no, it's you. Eggs are just too committed to the relationship. They want to stick around, literally. They're like clingy exes that won't leave your pan.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's why I'm breaking up with breakfast. We had a good run, but I need to see other meals. Toast? We're done. Bacon? Don't call me anymore.

jokes.text: Eddie makes eggs for Chandler a completely different way from how Joey used to. 'I thought you liked your eggs with the bread with the hole in the middle, à la me.'
jokes.setup: Eddie serves Chandler eggs; Joey watches, comparing to how he used to make them.
jokes.punchline: 'À la me' — Joey's possessive phrase about his egg style ('à la me') is both funny as a pretentious French flourish and devastating as a territorial claim over Chandler's breakfast preferences.
jokes.explanation: 'À la me' is a delightful small joke — Joey using culinary French to assert ownership over Chandler's breakfast routine. Works perfectly in the episode's breakup metaphor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? I think Ross and Monica are from a completely different dimension. Like, that's not normal sibling behavior—that's alien-level weird.

jokes.text: 'That's it! He just comes in here, Mr. Johnny New Eggs, with his moving the mail and his: [imitating Eddie] See you, pals.'
jokes.setup: After pretending to be fine, Joey can no longer contain his jealousy and rage about Eddie.
jokes.punchline: 'Mr. Johnny New Eggs' is a wonderful comic coinage — Joey's jealousy expressed through the lens of eggs and farewell phrases. The imitation of 'see you, pals' as if it's an outrage is perfectly petty.
jokes.explanation: 'Mr. Johnny New Eggs' is among the episode's best lines — a perfect Joey outburst that synthesizes multiple grievances into one absurd epithet. The mock-fury about 'see you, pals' is hilarious. This joke is highly quotable and deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: When Monica gets angry, her voice reaches a frequency of approximately 4,000 hertz, which is well into the ultrasonic range. It's actually fascinating from a purely scientific standpoint.

jokes.text: 'And now there's no juice! There's no juice for the people who need the juice. I need the juice!'
jokes.setup: Joey's rant about Eddie continues — he's been listing grievances.
jokes.punchline: The rant climaxes at 'I need the juice!' — escalating from legitimate grievances to a declaration about orange juice that sounds like political manifesto. Then there's literally another carton right there.
jokes.explanation: Escalation comedy at its best. 'I need the juice!' as the crescendo of a speech about romantic betrayal is funny because of how small it is — and because it's immediately punctured by the discovery of another carton. The triple repetition of 'juice' builds perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? It's not a big deal.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Not a big deal? Monica, you just said you...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes, I did. And I'd do it again.

jokes.text: 'There's another carton right over there.' [long beat] / 'Hey, this isn't about juice anymore, all right, man?'
jokes.setup: Joey just declared 'I need the juice!' as if it's a crisis.
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately spots another carton, deflating the drama. Joey's recovery — 'This isn't about juice anymore' — is both an admission and a laugh line, as the audience realizes it was never about juice.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedic deflation followed by an even better recovery. The one-two of 'there's another carton' → 'this isn't about juice anymore' is beautifully structured. The second line is the real punchline — Joey's self-aware pivot.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I mean, I love my parents, but there's a difference between obligatory love and actual hatred.

jokes.text: 'Whose eggs do you like better, his or mine?' / 'I like both eggs equally.' / 'Nobody likes two kinds of eggs equally. You like one better...' / 'What's the difference? Your eggs aren't here anymore. You took your eggs, and you left! Did you really expect me to never find new eggs?'
jokes.setup: Joey demands Chandler choose between his eggs and Eddie's eggs.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's eggs speech — 'You took your eggs and you left! Did you really expect me to never find new eggs?' — is the full romantic-breakup metaphor made explicit and passionate, about eggs. The absurdity of applying romantic language to breakfast food is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The episode's comedic high point for the Joey/Chandler storyline. The eggs-as-relationship metaphor reaches its fullest, most absurd expression here. 'Did you really expect me to never find new eggs?' is a line that completely sells the joke — it sounds like a real relationship speech. Near-perfect structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, she's like an unwanted shelter animal. Nobody wants her, she's got all these problems, and nobody knows what to do with her.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Kind of like my song 'Sticky Shoes.'

jokes.text: Meanwhile, Ross and Monica argue about the TV. 'I wanna watch Entertainment Tonight.' / 'Tough. We're watching Predators of the Serengeti.' / 'It's my TV!' / 'Bite me!'
jokes.setup: Ross and Monica are still cohabitating; Rachel is stuck in the middle.
jokes.punchline: 'Bite me!' — the argument has escalated to pure playground insults, continuing their childish regression.
jokes.explanation: Functional but weak continuation of the regression gag. 'Bite me' is a predictable childish insult that doesn't add much beyond what we've already seen. The bit is running a bit thin by this point.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I just realized something. That voice actress who does all those cartoons? She's been doing my songs! And I never even knew she was making them sound so... deep.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Like, when she sang 'Smelly Cat,' I thought it was just supposed to be silly, but she made it sound like it was actually about something meaningful!

jokes.text: Rachel declares she's going to take a bubble bath because 'you kids are driving me crazy' — framing herself as the put-upon parent.
jokes.setup: Ross and Monica are fighting like children while Rachel is stuck in the apartment.
jokes.punchline: Rachel adopts the parent role — announcing a bubble bath as her escape, calling them 'you kids.' The role reversal is the joke: Rachel, the least maternal of the three, is the adult in the room.
jokes.explanation: A solid structural joke — Rachel's parental exasperation works because she's the least likely person to be the responsible adult. The bubble bath detail is a nice character touch.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Baywatch is a masterpiece of television!

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: No, no, no. It's not a masterpiece. It's just... it's just a show about people running on a beach.

jokes.text: 'Mon, you've gone ultrasonic again, all right?'
jokes.setup: Monica is yelling at Ross and has apparently gotten very high-pitched.
jokes.punchline: 'Ultrasonic' — Ross's scientific vocabulary deployed as a sibling insult is perfectly Ross-specific. He's accusing her of going beyond human hearing range when she's angry.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific joke. 'Ultrasonic' is a perfect Ross word — it's scientific, slightly condescending, and deployed as a sibling insult. The economy is exceptional (one word does all the work). Could only be Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: Baywatch is so shallow. All it is is half-naked women running on a beach.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey! Hey, hey, hey. Those women are trained professionals. They're saving lives.

jokes.text: 'I hated you when we were kids.' / 'You hated me when we were kids?' / 'Yes. I hated you. I loved you in a you're-my-brother-so-I-have-to way, but basically I hated your guts.'
jokes.setup: Ross thought their childhood was fun and their fighting was playful. Monica sets him straight.
jokes.punchline: 'I loved you in a you're-my-brother-so-I-have-to way, but basically I hated your guts.' — The distinction Monica draws between obligatory love and genuine feeling is both real and very funny. Ross's shock is the reaction beat.
jokes.explanation: A strong joke that works on both comedic and emotional levels. 'I loved you in a you're-my-brother-so-I-have-to way' is an extremely precise and relatable parsing of sibling obligation vs. genuine affection. Ross's devastation makes the room laugh. Very quotable.

jokes.text: 'Because you were mean to me and you teased me and you always got your way.' / 'That wasn't fun for you?' / 'Uh-huh.'
jokes.setup: Monica explains why she hated Ross as a kid.
jokes.punchline: Ross's genuinely confused 'That wasn't fun for you?' — delivered as if bullying and teasing should logically be enjoyable for both parties — is a perfect moment of Ross's oblivious self-centeredness.
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly economical. Three words — 'That wasn't fun for you?' — perfectly capture Ross's self-centered perspective. He genuinely thought being teased was mutually fun. Monica's flat 'Uh-huh' is the perfect button. The line works because it's character-perfect.

jokes.text: 'That wasn't fun for you?' / 'Uh-huh.'
jokes.setup: Monica has listed all the ways Ross was mean to her as a child — teasing, always getting his way
jokes.punchline: Ross genuinely asks if that wasn't fun, as if the experience was mutual; Monica's flat 'Uh-huh' confirms it definitively was not
jokes.explanation: Ross's oblivious question reveals that he genuinely had no idea his bullying wasn't fun for Monica. The single 'Uh-huh' in response is perfectly understated. Good sibling comedy, though it serves the emotional beat more than the comedic one.

jokes.text: 'You're just gonna have to stop pissing me off.' / 'I can do that.' / 'Then I won't have to kill you.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Ross have just had an emotional moment where she admits she now loves him genuinely.
jokes.punchline: 'Then I won't have to kill you' — Monica's threat of murder as a loving postscript to a tender reconciliation is perfectly Monica-dark.
jokes.explanation: A nice button to the reconciliation scene. Monica threatening murder as an expression of familial love is characterful and funny. Not among the episode's strongest jokes but works well as a scene-ender.

jokes.text: 'The record company sent this paper for me to sign saying it's okay for someone else to sing for me. That was my first clue.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe reveals she figured out the voice on the Smelly Cat video wasn't hers.
jokes.punchline: 'That was my first clue' — delivered completely straight, as if identifying a legal document stipulating her own replacement as a clue is remarkable detective work.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Phoebe deadpan. The joke is the understatement — a signed document saying someone else is singing for her is described as merely the 'first clue,' implying Phoebe might have needed more evidence. Perfect character joke. Very economical.

jokes.text: 'Okay, Pheebs, but what about you?' / 'I have a video. Pay attention.'
jokes.setup: Rachel tries to redirect Phoebe's concern for 'the voice woman' back to Phoebe's own situation.
jokes.punchline: 'I have a video. Pay attention.' — Phoebe's complete literalism. Rachel meant 'what about your feelings/career' but Phoebe hears it as a factual question and corrects her.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest Phoebe jokes. The complete literalism — 'I have a video' as a rebuttal — is perfect character comedy. It's also impeccably economical (four words). The 'Pay attention' makes it even funnier — mildly scolding Rachel for asking a confusing question. Could only be Phoebe.

jokes.text: Phoebe compares the voice woman to unwanted pound animals — specifically 'some old dog who's kind of like stinky' — and then realizes: 'Oh, my God! She's Smelly Cat!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is describing the voice woman's plight using increasingly specific animal metaphors.
jokes.punchline: She accidentally describes the Smelly Cat song lyric — an unloved, stinky animal — and suddenly makes the connection: the voice woman IS smelly cat, the subject of the very song she's singing.
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. A beautifully constructed callback that brings together the Smelly Cat song and the voice woman's story in a way that feels both surprising and inevitable. Phoebe's genuine revelation is moving and funny simultaneously. 'Oh, my God! She's Smelly Cat!' is a perfect line. The follow-up — 'Oh, oh, that song has so many levels' — is an equally great button.

jokes.text: 'Oh, oh, that song has so many levels.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just realized the voice woman is metaphorically the Smelly Cat.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's awed declaration that 'Smelly Cat' — a simple, silly song about a smelly cat — has 'so many levels' is the perfect button. She's discovering depth in her own song that exists only in her imagination.
jokes.explanation: Six words that capture everything about Phoebe as a character. The joke is that 'Smelly Cat' manifestly does not have many levels — it's a song about a smelly cat — but Phoebe's ability to find profound meaning in it is simultaneously mocked and celebrated. Extremely quotable. A perfect Phoebe button.

jokes.text: Eddie says he's 'not really into sports' when Joey asks him to play foosball — treating a table game as a sport.
jokes.setup: Joey tries to bond with Eddie over foosball.
jokes.punchline: Eddie declines, calling himself not 'into sports' — using that word for foosball, and thereby signaling he's not a Joey-compatible roommate.
jokes.explanation: A functional joke establishing the Joey/Eddie incompatibility. The 'not into sports' for foosball is a mild chuckle. Not particularly crafted — it's more of a plot beat with a small joke attached.

jokes.text: Eddie says Baywatch is 'just pretty people running around on the beach.' Joey responds: 'Well, that's the brilliance of it.' Then: 'The pretty people. And the running.'
jokes.setup: Joey tries to get Eddie into Baywatch; Eddie dismisses it.
jokes.punchline: Joey uses the exact same logic he used with Chandler earlier ('the brilliance') but now with a stranger who doesn't get it — making the Baywatch enthusiasm feel lonelier and sadder. 'The pretty people. And the running.' mirrors his earlier 'Run like the wind.'
jokes.explanation: A beautifully sad callback. The same Baywatch speech that was funny and warm with Chandler is now hollow with Eddie, who doesn't share Joey's enthusiasm. The repetition of 'the running' highlights the contrast between roommates. Well-crafted structural callback.

jokes.text: After Eddie goes to his room, Joey sits alone in the living room and just chuckles to himself, then goes quiet — a reaction beat revealing his loneliness.
jokes.setup: Joey has just tried and failed to connect with Eddie over Baywatch.
jokes.punchline: Joey's small, hollow chuckle followed by silence — he's alone in the apartment that used to be his, sitting with a stranger's roommate. The laugh track would underline this as comedy, but the moment is bittersweet.
jokes.explanation: A quiet, effective moment. Not a big laugh but a well-observed comedic beat that plays on the gap between the warm energy of the Chandler scenes and the awkward quiet of the Eddie scenes. The economy is total — silence says everything.

jokes.text: The friends sing Smelly Cat together. Phoebe assigns solos — 'Monica... Chandler... Joey' — and when she gets to Ross: 'Ross, those are the only lines we have. Sorry. Okay. Back to the chorus.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe leads her friends in a group Smelly Cat singalong, assigning each person a line.
jokes.punchline: Ross gets to the mic with anticipation and is immediately told there are no more lines — she's already given them all away. The pause before 'Sorry. Okay. Back to the chorus.' is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: A sweet, funny ending. Phoebe's casual 'Sorry. Okay.' as she cuts Ross off is perfectly Phoebe — no malice, just the facts. The warm group singalong as the episode's close is tonally perfect, and Ross's exclusion is a good final laugh.

tmdb_overview: Phoebe is discovered by a record producer who wants to make "Smelly Cat" a video. Ross's new relationship with Rachel makes Monica feel like she's living with her brother again... and she hates it.  And Joey considers moving back in with Chandler, but Chandler has a new roommate.
insight: Roommate friction generates steady laughs, but 2.6 jokes-per-minute feels slight for a setup-heavy episode.
